p: Swete prints "with her hair let down" from Venetus; Alexandrinus itself has "the wars let loose."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (from Codex Venetus), and Rahlfs
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete in his footnote

why: Loosened hair is the sign of a woman in mourning or pleading, and it fits the tears and wailing beside it. "The wars" (polemous, a few letters from plokamous) makes no sense with "let loose" said of a woman, so Swete corrected Alexandrinus from Venetus.

t: The faithful God or the Most Great God?
p: Alexandrinus calls God "faithful" here; Venetus, and Rahlfs, have the book's usual title "the Most Great God."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton's English ("the Greatest God")

why: The Plain keeps the base text. "Most Great God" is the book's stock title (1:16; 3:11), so a copyist could easily have brought it in here; but the same habit could have pushed a copyist the other way, and Rahlfs chose it. The meaning of the scene is the same either way.

p: Alexandrinus says the king was struck by the place's devotion; Venetus and Rahlfs say by its splendor.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text

why: The two Greek words differ by a few letters (eusebeia, euprepeia). Both make sense: the king admires the worship he sees, or the look of the building. The Plain keeps the base text.

t: Not even Gentiles, or not even Jews?
p: Alexandrinus says no Gentile may enter; Venetus and Rahlfs say no one "of the nation," that is, no Jew.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: because not even the nations (may) enter

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes ("of the nation"); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text (adds "is allowed"); Brenton ("none of the nation")
readings.orig: μηδὲ τοῖς ἐκ τοῦ ἔθνους ἐξεῖναι εἰσιέναι
readings.en: because not even those of the nation are allowed to enter
readings.plain: No one of our nation may go in

why: The Plain keeps the base text, but the other reading may well be older: the point of the answer is that even most Jews, and most priests, may not enter, so how much less a Gentile king. In Alexandrinus the steps run Gentiles, then priests, then the high priest.

a: what reason is there that I should not enter all of them
p: Swete's Greek has "of all"; Rahlfs reads "by all means," one letter different.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (Codex Venetus has a third form, pantes, all people, from Swete's footnotes)
readings.orig: διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν οὐχὶ πάντων εἰσελεύσεσθαι
readings.en: for what reason (should I) not enter of all
readings.plain: what reason is there that I should not enter all of them

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
readings.orig: διά τινα αἰτίαν οὐχὶ πάντως εἰσελεύσεσθαι
readings.en: for what reason (should I) not by all means enter
readings.plain: what reason is there that I should not go in anyway

why: Pantōn ("of all") and pantōs ("by all means") differ by one letter. Swete's text is awkward Greek, which may be why Rahlfs corrected it; the king's point is the same: no one will stop him.

a: They even made the streets full of groaning
p: Alexandrinus has a small word meaning "even"; Venetus and Rahlfs have "wailing."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: πού γε καὶ στεναγμῶν ἐνεμπίπλων τὰς πλατείας
readings.en: and indeed they filled the streets with groans
readings.plain: They even made the streets full of groaning

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
readings.orig: γόου τε καὶ στεναγμῶν ἐνεπίμπλων τὰς πλατείας
readings.en: and they filled the streets with wailing and groans
readings.plain: They made the streets full of wailing and groaning

why: The two readings look alike in Greek capitals (POUGE, GOOUTE). Venetus's "wailing" pairs well with "groans" and is probably right, but the base text is readable, so the Plain keeps it.

a: deserted the wedding rooms prepared for them
p: Swete's text has no noun here; Rahlfs prints "the bridal chambers prepared for the wedding procession." The Plain follows Rahlfs.

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton ("left their bridal chambers")
readings.en: the bridal chambers prepared for the meeting
readings.plain: deserted the wedding rooms prepared for them

readings.w: Swete's printed text (A, with Swete's spelling of the last word; Swete's footnotes give no other word for V)
readings.plain: left behind all that had been arranged for them

why: In Swete's Greek the article "those" is masculine but has no noun to go with it, which suggests a word has dropped out. Rahlfs's text supplies it (pastous, "bridal chambers") and reads "for the meeting" (the wedding procession) where Swete has "for everything now." This is a departure from the base text.

p: Venetus and Rahlfs add "in the city"; Alexandrinus says only that they ran in disorder. Goes with the variant before it.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
readings.en: a disorderly race in the city

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete

why: The Plain follows Rahlfs's text through this verse (see the variant on the wedding rooms). The words add nothing the scene does not already imply.

t: By the law, or for the law?
p: Swete's Greek has "under" the ancestral law; Rahlfs prints "for" it.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (A; Swete's footnotes record no difference in V here)
Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
readings.en: on behalf of the ancestral law

why: Hypo ("under, by") and hyper ("for") are easily confused. "For the law" is the usual phrase for martyrs (2 Maccabees 7:9), and Rahlfs adopts it. The Plain keeps the base text, which can mean dying as the law requires.

a: Then Simon the high priest knelt down facing the sanctuary. He stretched out his hands in the proper way and prayed like this:
p: Swete's text, from Alexandrinus, has no verse 2:1, so Simon's prayer begins with no speaker. Rahlfs's text and Brenton have it.

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton's English has the same verse
readings.orig: ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀρχιερεὺς Σιμων ἐξ ἐναντίας τοῦ ναοῦ κάμψας τὰ γόνατα καὶ τὰς χεῖρας προτείνας εὐτάκτως ἐποιήσατο τὴν δέησιν τοιαύτην
readings.en: So the high priest Simon, facing the sanctuary, bending his knees and stretching out his hands in good order, made a prayer like this
readings.plain: Then Simon the high priest knelt down facing the sanctuary. He stretched out his hands in the proper way and prayed like this:

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus); Swete's footnotes say nothing at 2:1

why: Without the verse the prayer of 2:2-20 has no speaker, and 2:21 speaks of "the prayer" as if someone had been named. So the Plain translates the verse from Rahlfs's Greek.
b: Swete's printed page, the digital copies of it, and his footnotes all skip 2:1 (the texts file marks it as a gap). Brenton's English (1844) has the verse: "Now was it that the high priest Simon bowed his knees over against the holy place" and prayed.

a: their wicked ways were plain for all to see
p: Alexandrinus says the Sodomites became "unseen" in their wickedness; Venetus and Rahlfs say "conspicuous." The Plain follows Venetus.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes (as far as the page can be read); Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton ("notorious")
readings.en: having become conspicuous in their vices
readings.plain: their wicked ways were plain for all to see

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (Swete's text)
readings.en: having become unseen (obscure) in their vices
readings.plain: their wicked ways were hidden from sight

why: The two words differ only by the letters di-. "Hidden" does not fit a city whose sin is the byword of the Bible (Genesis 18:20; Ezekiel 16:49), and "conspicuous" sets up "an example to later generations." This is a departure from the base text.

a: made your power known. By them you made your great might known.
p: Venetus lacks the words "your power ... you made known," so its Pharaoh line says it once.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
readings.orig: ἐγνώρισας τὴν σὴν δύναμιν, ἐφ᾽ αἷς ἐγνώρισας τὸ μέγα σου κράτος
readings.en: you made known your power, by which you made known your great might
readings.plain: made your power known. By them you made your great might known.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Brenton's English agrees
readings.en: you made known your great might

why: Venetus's copyist probably skipped from the first "you made known" to the second, an easy slip. The doubled line is the harder text and is kept.

p: Alexandrinus says "our place"; Rahlfs prints "this place."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton ("this house")

why: Simon is praying in the temple, so "this place" fits, as in 2:9, 14 and 16; but "our place" is the base text and means the same temple.

p: Alexandrinus and Venetus both say "others"; Swete and Rahlfs print "companions," a one-letter change.

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnotes

why: Hetairōn ("companions") and heterōn ("others") sounded alike when the Greek was copied. "Drinking partners and companions" is a natural pair; "drinking partners and others" is weak. Here Swete's printed text is not the codex: he corrected both manuscripts.

a: some of them came to be seen as hateful
t: Some seemed hateful, or seemed hateful to some?
p: Swete's text says "some appeared hateful"; Rahlfs reads "they appeared hateful to some."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (V agrees, as far as Swete's footnotes show)
readings.plain: some of them came to be seen as hateful

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton ("some persons held them in odium")
readings.plain: some people came to see them as hateful

why: The two differ by one letter (enioi, eniois). Rahlfs's reading fits the next verse better ("everyone thought well of them"), since it limits the hatred to a few outsiders; the base text is kept and can mean the same thing loosely.

p: Alexandrinus says the slanderers pinned "no small fear" on the Jews; Venetus and Rahlfs say "no small blame."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton ("much odium")

why: Phobos ("fear") and psogos ("blame") look alike in Greek capitals. "Blame" suits slander better; "fear" makes the Jews into a feared threat, which is the point of 3:7. The base text is kept.

a: we were glad to be good to them
p: Both codices read a phrase that makes no sense here; Swete and Rahlfs print "gladly."

readings.w: Swete's printed text; Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text
readings.plain: we were glad to be good to them

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus, from Swete's footnotes

why: Asmenōs ("gladly") lost its first letters in both manuscripts, leaving men hōs ("indeed as"), which breaks the sentence. Swete's printed text is not the codex here.

a: to make them partners with our priests for all time
t: Our priests, our rites, or nothing
p: Alexandrinus says "partners with the priests"; Rahlfs reads "sharers in the rites"; Venetus lacks the words.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: to make them partners with our priests for all time

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition of the Septuagint (1935), read in its digital text; Brenton ("the everlasting rites of our solemnities")
readings.plain: to make them sharers in our rites for all time

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s–800s AD), from Swete's footnotes ("om και μετοχους…καταστησαι V")

why: Hiereōn ("priests") and hierōn ("rites, sacred things") differ by one letter. Either way the offer is to draw the Jews into the king's own cult, the same bargain as 2:30. The base text is kept.
